item.title: Agentry: Building AI Agents as React Components with JSX
item.description: Agentry is a TypeScript framework that lets you define AI agents as React components using JSX — declarative, composable, and type-safe agent orchestration.
item.content:encoded:
What Is Agentry? A Framework That Treats AI Agents as React Components

Agentry is an open-source TypeScript framework that reimagines AI agents as React components. Instead of writing imperative agent logic with chained API calls and manual state management, you define agents declaratively using JSX — the same syntax React developers use for UI components. An agent becomes a tree of <Agent>, <System>, <Tools>, and <Message> elements rendered by a custom React reconciler. Created as a Thanksgiving 2025 weekend project by Colin Dsouza, Agentry is at version 0.1.0 with 8 GitHub stars and roughly 20 monthly npm downloads. Despite its early stage, the framework introduces a genuinely novel paradigm: using React’s component model not just to render UI, but to define the agent itself.

Core Architecture — How React’s Component Model Maps to Agent Execution

At the heart of Agentry is the react-reconciler package (v0.33), the same low-level library that powers React DOM and React Native. Agentry implements a custom host config that maps React’s reconciliation cycle — mount, update, unmount — to agent lifecycle events. When you write <Agent> in JSX, the reconciler creates a host instance that manages an LLM conversation loop. When a <Tool> mounts, the reconciler registers a function call handler. When it unmounts, the tool is removed from the agent’s available tool set.

This architecture means every React concept you already know — props, state, effects, context, conditional rendering — maps directly to agent behavior. The component tree becomes the agent execution tree. State changes trigger re-renders that update the agent’s system prompt, tool list, or message history. The framework uses Zustand for internal state management and eventemitter3 for event handling during execution.

Key Features Deep Dive

Declarative Agent Definition with JSX

Agentry’s most distinctive feature is its JSX-based agent definition. Here is what a basic agent looks like:

import { Agent, System, Tools, Tool, Message } from "agentry";

function MyAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>
        You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.
      </System>
      <Tools>
        <Tool name="search" parameters={searchSchema}>
          Perform web searches
        </Tool>
        <Tool name="calculator" parameters={calcSchema}>
          Perform mathematical calculations
        </Tool>
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

This declarative approach eliminates boilerplate. The <System> component sets the system prompt. <Tools> wraps tool definitions. Each <Tool> declares a name, Zod schema for parameters, and a description. The framework handles serialization, function calling, and response parsing automatically.

Dynamic Tools via React State

Because agents are React components, you can use useState to add or remove tools dynamically based on conversation context. This is a significant departure from static tool definitions in frameworks like LangChain or the Vercel AI SDK:

function AdaptiveAgent() {
  const [hasFileAccess, setHasFileAccess] = useState(false);

  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>You are a file management assistant.</System>
      <Tools>
        <Tool name="read_file" parameters={readFileSchema}>
          Read file contents
        </Tool>
        {hasFileAccess && (
          <Tool name="delete_file" parameters={deleteFileSchema}>
            Delete files from disk
          </Tool>
        )}
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

When hasFileAccess becomes true, the delete_file tool mounts and becomes available to the LLM on the next turn. When it becomes false, the tool unmounts and the agent can no longer call it. This pattern enables fine-grained, context-aware tool access control without any imperative tool registration logic.

Subagents and Composition with AgentTool

Agentry supports hierarchical agent composition through the <AgentTool> component. You can nest agents inside other agents, with type-safe parameter passing via Zod schemas:

function ResearchAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>Coordinate research across specialists.</System>
      <Tools>
        <AgentTool
          name="web_researcher"
          agent={<WebSearchAgent />}
          parameters={z.object({ query: z.string() })}
        />
        <AgentTool
          name="data_analyst"
          agent={<DataAnalysisAgent />}
          parameters={z.object({ dataset: z.string() })}
        />
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

The parent agent calls subagents as tools. Each subagent runs its own conversation loop with its own system prompt, tools, and model configuration. The parent receives the subagent’s final output as the tool result. This mirrors the manager-employee pattern common in production agent deployments.

Conditional Rendering with Condition

Agentry includes a <Condition> component that evaluates natural language conditions against conversation history to change agent behavior:

function CustomerSupportAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>You are a customer support agent.</System>
      <Condition when="the user is frustrated or angry">
        <System>Escalate to a human supervisor and apologize.</System>
        <Tool name="escalate" parameters={escalateSchema}>
          Escalate to human support
        </Tool>
      </Condition>
      <Condition when="the user asks about pricing">
        <System>Provide pricing information from our current plans.</System>
        <Tool name="lookup_pricing" parameters={pricingSchema}>
          Look up current pricing
        </Tool>
      </Condition>
    </Agent>
  );
}

The <Condition when="natural language description"> component evaluates the condition against the conversation history using an LLM call. When the condition is met, the children mount and become active. When it is not, they unmount. This enables natural language routing — a more flexible alternative to rigid if/else logic in agent code.

Programmatic Agent Spawning

Beyond declarative composition, Agentry provides context.runAgent() for programmatic agent spawning from within tool handlers. This enables parallel execution patterns:

async function researchTask({ queries }, context) {
  const results = await Promise.all(
    queries.map((q) =>
      context.runAgent(
        <WebSearchAgent query={q} />,
        { provider: "openai", model: "gpt-4o-mini" }
      )
    )
  );
  return synthesize(results);
}

This pattern is powerful for parallelizable workloads — analyzing multiple documents, searching across sources, or running independent validation checks simultaneously. Each spawned agent runs in its own execution context with its own conversation state.

Cross-Provider Subagents

Agentry supports mixing different LLM providers in the same agent tree. An OpenAI parent agent can spawn Anthropic subagents and vice versa:

function HybridAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>Coordinate research across providers.</System>
      <Tools>
        <AgentTool
          name="claude_analyst"
          agent={
            <Agent provider="anthropic" model="claude-sonnet-4">
              <System>Analyze data with deep reasoning.</System>
            </Agent>
          }
          parameters={z.object({ data: z.string() })}
        />
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

This cross-provider capability is rare among agent frameworks. Most frameworks lock you into a single provider. Agentry’s provider-agnostic reconciler means each subagent can use the model best suited to its task — GPT-4o for tool use, Claude for reasoning, a smaller model for classification — all within a single declarative tree.

Streaming and WebSocket Mode

Agentry supports both batch mode (run to completion and return the final result) and interactive mode (streaming responses with an ongoing conversation handle). For OpenAI, it offers WebSocket mode that reduces latency in multi-tool loops by maintaining a persistent connection. The framework also includes compaction controls for long conversations — you can configure when and how aggressively to summarize older messages to stay within context limits. Anthropic’s prompt caching is supported out of the box.

Comparison with Alternatives

Feature Agentry Tambo Vercel AI SDK
Approach Agents as React components Agents render React components Generative UI + agent tools
Stars 8 11,157 25,910
npm downloads/month ~20 Thousands Millions
Release v0.1.0 (Dec 2025) v1.0 (Feb 2026) v4.x (stable)
JSX agent definition Yes — core paradigm No No
Dynamic tools via state Yes — React useState No Limited
Subagents Yes — AgentTool + runAgent Yes Via AI SDK
Cross-provider Yes — mix OpenAI/Anthropic No Yes
Conditional routing Yes — Condition component No No
Streaming Yes — batch + interactive Yes Yes
WebSocket mode Yes (OpenAI) No Yes
Prompt caching Yes (Anthropic) Yes Yes
Maturity Experimental Production-ready Production-ready

Tambo — Agents That Render React Components

Tambo (11,157 stars) takes the opposite approach from Agentry. Instead of agents being React components, Tambo gives agents the ability to render React components. An agent decides which UI component to show based on conversation context, and Tambo handles the state management between the user, the agent, and the rendered component. Tambo has processed over half a million messages on its hosted service and reached v1.0 in February 2026. It is significantly more mature than Agentry and has an active community.

Vercel AI SDK — The Industry Standard

The Vercel AI SDK (25,910 stars) is the dominant toolkit for building AI-powered applications in the TypeScript ecosystem. Created by the team behind Next.js, it supports generative UI — agents that dynamically render React components — alongside streaming, tool calling, and multi-model support. It is framework-agnostic (React, Svelte, Vue, Next.js) and production-tested at scale. For most teams, the Vercel AI SDK is the safe, proven choice.

Agent Prism and Gaia UI — Visualization and UI Libraries

Agent Prism (376 stars) by Evil Martians focuses on observability — visualizing AI agent traces using OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing of LLM calls. Gaia UI (212 stars) provides beautifully designed React components for building agent interfaces. Neither competes directly with Agentry; they solve different problems in the agent development stack.

Practical Evaluation — Installation, Setup, and First Impressions

Agentry requires React 19 and Zod 4 as peer dependencies, plus either the Anthropic or OpenAI SDK depending on your provider. Installation is straightforward:

npm install agentry

The framework ships as a single small package with minimal dependencies: react-reconciler, zustand, eventemitter3, and scheduler. The API surface is compact — you can learn the core concepts in under 30 minutes if you already know React and TypeScript.

However, documentation is sparse. The README on GitHub provides examples but no API reference, no migration guide, and no troubleshooting section. There are no tests visible in the repository, no CI/CD pipeline, and no contribution guidelines. For a framework at v0.1.0, this is expected but worth noting.

Use Cases and When to Use Agentry

Agentry’s declarative, component-based approach shines in specific scenarios:

  • Complex agent hierarchies — When you need manager agents that delegate to specialist subagents with different models and tools
  • Dynamic tool access control — When tool availability depends on context, authentication state, or user role
  • Multi-provider agent systems — When different subtasks benefit from different LLM providers
  • Experimental and research projects — When you want to explore novel agent composition patterns
  • React-centric teams — When your team already thinks in components and wants to apply that mental model to agents

For production applications serving real users, Tambo or the Vercel AI SDK are safer choices today. Agentry is best suited for exploration, prototyping, and understanding what declarative agent composition looks like in practice.

Limitations and Maturity Concerns

Agentry’s biggest limitation is its maturity. With 8 GitHub stars, 20 monthly npm downloads, and no visible test suite, the framework is effectively an experimental prototype. Key concerns include:

  • No production deployments — No evidence of the framework running in production
  • Single maintainer — Colin Dsouza is the sole contributor; bus factor of 1
  • No test coverage — No tests visible in the repository
  • No documentation beyond README — No API docs, no examples directory, no guides
  • React 19 requirement — Teams on React 18 cannot adopt Agentry without upgrading
  • Zod 4 requirement — Zod 4 is still in early adoption; many projects use Zod 3
  • No error handling guidance — How does the framework handle provider failures, rate limits, or malformed tool calls?
  • No streaming reliability guarantees — WebSocket reconnection, backpressure, and error recovery are undocumented

Verdict — Is Agentry Worth Adopting?

Agentry is one of the most interesting experimental agent frameworks in the TypeScript ecosystem. Its core insight — that React’s component model maps naturally to agent composition — is genuinely novel and could influence how future agent frameworks are designed. The ability to define agents with JSX, manage tools with useState, compose subagents declaratively, and mix providers in a single tree is powerful.

However, Agentry is not production-ready. At v0.1.0 with 8 stars and no test coverage, it is a proof of concept — a glimpse of what declarative agent composition could look like, not a tool for building production systems. For teams building agent-powered applications today, the Vercel AI SDK or Tambo are the right choices. For teams curious about where agent frameworks are heading, Agentry is worth watching — and perhaps contributing to.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Agentry and how does it work?

Agentry is a TypeScript framework that lets you define AI agents as React components using JSX syntax. It uses React’s reconciler to render agent execution trees, mapping React’s component lifecycle to agent lifecycle events. Agents are composed declaratively with components like <Agent>, <System>, <Tools>, and <Message>.

How is Agentry different from the Vercel AI SDK?

The Vercel AI SDK provides tools for building AI-powered applications with generative UI — agents that can render React components. Agentry takes the opposite approach: the agent itself is a React component. Agentry also supports JSX-based agent definitions, dynamic tool mounting via React state, and cross-provider subagents as first-class features.

Does Agentry support multiple LLM providers?

Yes. Agentry supports both OpenAI and Anthropic providers through a single declarative API. It also supports cross-provider subagents — an OpenAI parent agent can spawn Anthropic subagents and vice versa. Each subagent in the tree can use a different provider and model.

Is Agentry ready for production use?

No. Agentry is at version 0.1.0 with 8 GitHub stars, approximately 20 monthly npm downloads, no visible test suite, and a single maintainer. It is best suited for experimentation, prototyping, and research. For production applications, consider the Vercel AI SDK or Tambo.

What are the prerequisites for using Agentry?

Agentry requires React 19 and Zod 4 as peer dependencies, plus either the Anthropic SDK or OpenAI SDK depending on your chosen provider. The framework itself has minimal dependencies: react-reconciler, zustand, eventemitter3, and scheduler.

item.title: Awesome LLM Apps 2026: 100+ Open-Source AI Agents and RAG Apps You Can Clone and Ship Today
item.description: Discover 100+ open-source AI agents and RAG apps from the #1 GitHub repo with 128K+ stars. Clone, customize, and deploy production-ready LLM apps today.
item.content:encoded:
The awesome LLM apps 2026 ecosystem is dominated by a single GitHub repository — Shubhamsaboo/awesome-llm-apps — that has amassed 128,721 stars and 18,997 forks as of July 2026. It offers over 100 hand-built, end-to-end tested AI agents, agent skills, and RAG applications across 15 categories, all under the Apache-2.0 license, meaning you can clone, customize, and even sell what you build without legal friction.

What Is Awesome LLM Apps? — The #1 Open-Source AI Agent Collection

Awesome LLM Apps is the largest curated collection of open-source LLM applications on GitHub. Created in April 2024, the repository has grown from a handful of demo scripts into a comprehensive library spanning 15 categories of AI agent templates. Unlike many open-source projects that offer only documentation or toy examples, every template in this repo is hand-built, tested end-to-end, and designed to work out of the box with minimal configuration.

The repo supports over 10 LLM providers including Claude, Gemini, GPT, DeepSeek, Llama, Qwen, Grok, Cohere, and Gemma. This provider-agnostic design means you are never locked into a single model — you can swap backends with a single environment variable change.

Why 128K+ Stars? — What Makes This Repo Different

Several factors explain the explosive growth of awesome-llm-apps to become the #1 repository of the day on Trendshift:

Production-ready, not just educational. Each template is a complete, runnable application with proper error handling, configuration management, and deployment instructions. Developers can go from git clone to a working AI agent in under 60 seconds.

Apache-2.0 license. The permissive license removes all barriers to commercial use. Startups, agencies, and enterprises can fork the repo, build proprietary products on top of the templates, and ship to production without legal review or royalty obligations.

15 categories covering the full AI stack. From single-file starter agents to multi-agent teams with 5+ specialized agents working together, the repo covers every major pattern in modern LLM application development.

Active maintenance and community contributions. With nearly 19,000 forks, the community continuously contributes new templates, bug fixes, and improvements. The maintainers actively review pull requests and keep templates updated with the latest API changes from LLM providers.

Quick Start — Run Your First AI Agent in 30 Seconds

Getting started with awesome-llm-apps requires only Python 3.10+ and an API key from any supported LLM provider:

git clone https://github.com/Shubhamsaboo/awesome-llm-apps.git
cd awesome-llm-apps
pip install -r requirements.txt
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-api-key"
python ai_agents/starter_agents/smart_assistant.py

That is it. The smart assistant agent will begin responding to queries with full conversational memory, tool use, and multi-step reasoning. For developers who prefer a visual interface, many templates include Streamlit or Gradio frontends that launch automatically.

Category 1 — Agent Skills: Give Your Coding Agent Superpowers

Agent Skills represent a new paradigm in AI development. Instead of building custom integrations for every tool, developers can install pre-built skills via a single command:

npx skills add

These skills work with Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Cursor — the three most popular AI coding assistants. Each skill gives the coding agent a new capability: web scraping, database querying, API integration, file system operations, and more. The skill ecosystem means developers can extend their coding agents without writing a single line of integration code.

Category 2 — Starter AI Agents: Single-File, Zero-Friction

The starter agents category contains the simplest templates — single Python files that demonstrate core AI agent patterns. These include:

  • Smart Assistant — conversational agent with memory and tool use
  • Research Assistant — web-browsing agent that synthesizes information from multiple sources
  • Code Generator — agent that writes, tests, and debugs code iteratively
  • Data Analyzer — agent that processes CSV files and generates visualizations

Each starter agent is under 200 lines of code, making them ideal learning resources for developers new to AI agent development.

Category 3 — Advanced AI Agents: Production-Ready Multi-Step Reasoning

Advanced agents handle complex, multi-step workflows that require planning, tool selection, and error recovery. These templates include:

  • Financial Analyst Agent — analyzes market data, generates reports, and makes predictions
  • Legal Document Reviewer — reads contracts, identifies clauses, and suggests revisions
  • Medical Research Agent — searches medical literature, summarizes findings, and checks for drug interactions
  • Code Review Agent — performs automated code reviews with style checking, security analysis, and performance recommendations

These agents use advanced prompting techniques like chain-of-thought reasoning, ReAct (Reasoning + Acting), and self-reflection to improve output quality.

Category 4 — Multi-Agent Teams: Swarms of Specialists

Multi-agent teams are the dominant pattern in the awesome-llm-apps 2026 collection, with over 10 templates dedicated to team-based architectures. Each team consists of specialized agents that collaborate on complex tasks:

Team Template Agents Use Case
Finance Team Analyst, Researcher, Writer, Reviewer Investment research and reporting
Legal Team Contract Reviewer, Case Researcher, Compliance Checker, Document Drafter Legal document processing
Real Estate Team Property Analyzer, Market Researcher, Buyer Agent, Negotiation Agent Property transactions
Recruitment Team Job Scraper, Resume Analyzer, Interview Scheduler, Skills Assessor End-to-end hiring
Game Design Team Concept Designer, Mechanic Designer, Level Builder, Playtester Game development

Each agent in a team has a specific role, access to different tools, and a communication protocol for sharing information. The orchestrator agent manages the workflow, delegates subtasks, and synthesizes the final output.

Category 5 — Voice AI Agents: Speech-In, Speech-Out

Voice AI agents are the fastest-growing category in the repository. These templates integrate real-time speech recognition and synthesis to create voice-enabled applications:

  • Customer Support Voice Agent — handles inbound calls, answers FAQs, and escalates complex issues
  • Insurance Claims Agent — guides users through claim filing with voice interaction
  • Healthcare Triage Agent — collects symptoms, assesses urgency, and schedules appointments
  • Audio Tour Guide — provides location-aware audio tours with natural conversation

These agents use real-time voice APIs from providers like ElevenLabs, Deepgram, and AssemblyAI, combined with LLM reasoning for natural conversation flow.

Category 6 — RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): From Basic to Agentic

The repository includes over 20 RAG tutorials that progress from basic implementations to advanced agentic patterns:

Basic RAG — Simple retrieve-and-generate pipeline using vector search with OpenAI embeddings and ChromaDB.

Advanced RAG — Chunking strategies, metadata filtering, hybrid search (vector + keyword), and re-ranking for improved retrieval quality.

Agentic RAG — The agent decides when to retrieve, what queries to run, and whether the retrieved information is sufficient. Key patterns include:

  • Self-Grading RAG — the agent evaluates retrieved documents for relevance and re-queries if results are insufficient
  • Corrective RAG — the agent detects hallucinations or contradictions in retrieved content and corrects them
  • Hybrid Search RAG — combines vector similarity search with keyword search (BM25) for comprehensive retrieval
  • Knowledge Graph RAG — extracts entities and relationships from documents, builds a knowledge graph, and queries it alongside vector search
RAG Pattern Retrieval Method Best For
Basic RAG Vector search only Simple Q&A on small document sets
Advanced RAG Hybrid search + re-ranking Enterprise document search
Agentic RAG Self-grading + corrective retrieval Complex research and analysis
Knowledge Graph RAG Graph + vector search Multi-entity relationship queries

Category 7 — MCP AI Agents: Tool Integration via Model Context Protocol

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is becoming the standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources. The repository includes 6+ MCP agent templates that demonstrate:

  • GitHub MCP Agent — reads repositories, creates issues, reviews pull requests, and manages projects
  • Notion MCP Agent — queries and updates Notion databases, pages, and properties
  • Browser MCP Agent — controls a headless browser for web automation and data extraction
  • Travel MCP Agent — searches flights, hotels, and activities via travel APIs
  • Database MCP Agent — executes SQL queries, explores schemas, and generates reports

MCP provides a standardized interface that decouples agent logic from tool implementations. Any MCP-compatible tool can be swapped in without changing the agent code.

Category 8 — Generative UI: Agents That Build Interfaces

Generative UI agents represent an emerging paradigm where AI agents render interactive visual components — not just text responses. These templates produce:

  • Kanban Boards — agents that create and manage project boards with drag-and-drop functionality
  • Dashboards — real-time data dashboards with charts, tables, and filters
  • Form Builders — dynamic forms that adapt based on user input
  • Chat Interfaces — custom chat UIs with markdown rendering, code highlighting, and file uploads

This category bridges the gap between conversational AI and traditional web applications, enabling agents to deliver rich, interactive experiences without requiring a separate frontend development effort.

Category 9 — Always-On Agents: Background Automation

Always-on agents run on schedules, monitoring data sources and delivering results proactively. These templates include:

  • Daily Briefing Agent — summarizes news, emails, and calendar events each morning
  • Price Monitor Agent — tracks product prices and alerts when targets are met
  • Social Media Monitor Agent — watches for brand mentions and sentiment changes
  • Competitor Watch Agent — tracks competitor websites, pricing changes, and product launches

These agents use cron-based scheduling and can deliver results via email, Slack, SMS, or webhook. They are designed to run on low-cost infrastructure like a $5/month VPS or a Raspberry Pi.

Category 10 — LLM Apps with Memory: Cross-Session Personalization

Memory is a key differentiator in the awesome-llm-apps 2026 collection. Templates in this category implement persistent, cross-session memory for personalization:

  • Conversation Memory — stores chat history and user preferences across sessions
  • Entity Memory — remembers facts about people, places, and things mentioned in conversations
  • Procedural Memory — learns user workflows and preferences over time
  • Episodic Memory — recalls past interactions and their outcomes

Memory implementations use vector databases (ChromaDB, Pinecone, Weaviate) for semantic retrieval and SQLite for structured data. The memory layer enables agents to provide increasingly personalized responses as they accumulate user history.

Category 11 — LLM Optimization & Fine-Tuning: Cut Costs, Boost Quality

This category focuses on making LLM applications more efficient and cost-effective:

  • Prompt Caching — reduces API costs by caching common prompt patterns
  • Response Streaming — improves user experience with real-time token-by-token output
  • Model Routing — sends simple queries to cheaper models and complex queries to premium models
  • Fine-Tuning Templates — scripts for fine-tuning open-source models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) on custom datasets
  • Quantization Guides — reduce model size and inference cost by 50-80% with minimal quality loss

These optimization techniques can reduce API costs by 60-90% in production deployments while maintaining or improving response quality.

Category 12 — AI Agent Framework Crash Courses: ADK, OpenAI SDK, and More

The repository includes crash courses for the major AI agent frameworks:

  • Google ADK (Agent Development Kit) — Google’s framework for building production agents with tool use and multi-agent orchestration
  • OpenAI Agents SDK — OpenAI’s official SDK for building agents with GPT models
  • LangChain / LangGraph — the most popular open-source framework for chaining LLM calls
  • LlamaIndex — data framework optimized for RAG applications
  • CrewAI — framework for orchestrating role-based multi-agent teams
  • AutoGen — Microsoft’s multi-agent conversation framework
  • Mastra — TypeScript-native agent framework
  • PydanticAI — Python agent framework built on Pydantic for type-safe agent development

Each crash course includes a complete working example, explanation of key concepts, and deployment instructions.

How to Choose the Right Template for Your Project

Your Goal Recommended Category Example Template
Learn AI agent basics Starter AI Agents Smart Assistant
Build a customer support bot Voice AI Agents Customer Support Voice Agent
Automate research workflows Advanced AI Agents Research Agent
Deploy a multi-agent system Multi-Agent Teams Finance Team
Add RAG to your app RAG Tutorials Agentic RAG
Connect to external tools MCP AI Agents GitHub MCP Agent
Build interactive UIs Generative UI Dashboard Builder
Run background automation Always-On Agents Daily Briefing Agent
Add personalization Memory Agents Entity Memory Agent
Reduce API costs LLM Optimization Model Router

The Future of Open-Source LLM Apps in 2026 and Beyond

The awesome-llm-apps repository reflects several major trends shaping the AI development landscape in 2026:

Multi-agent architectures are becoming the default. Single-agent systems are giving way to teams of specialized agents that collaborate on complex tasks. The repository’s 10+ multi-agent team templates represent the fastest-growing category.

Voice is the new interface. Voice AI agents are moving from novelty to necessity, with real-time voice APIs enabling natural customer interactions across industries.

MCP is standardizing tool integration. The Model Context Protocol is emerging as the universal connector between AI agents and external systems, reducing integration effort and increasing interoperability.

Generative UI is blurring the line between chatbots and web apps. Agents that render interactive interfaces are opening new possibilities for AI-native applications.

RAG continues to mature. From basic retrieval to agentic, self-grading, and knowledge-graph-enhanced systems, RAG patterns are becoming more sophisticated and reliable.

The barrier to entry has never been lower. With 100+ production-ready templates under an Apache-2.0 license, any developer can build and deploy AI applications without starting from scratch.

FAQ

What is awesome LLM apps 2026?

Awesome LLM Apps 2026 refers to the Shubhamsaboo/awesome-llm-apps GitHub repository, the largest open-source collection of AI agent templates with 128,721 stars. It contains over 100 hand-built, end-to-end tested AI agents, agent skills, and RAG applications across 15 categories, all under the Apache-2.0 license.

Can I use awesome-llm-apps templates for commercial projects?

Yes. The repository is licensed under Apache-2.0, which grants permission to use, modify, distribute, and sell derivative works without royalty payments. This makes it ideal for startups, agencies, and enterprises building commercial AI products.

What LLM providers does awesome-llm-apps support?

The repository supports over 10 LLM providers including OpenAI (GPT), Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), DeepSeek, Meta (Llama), Alibaba (Qwen), xAI (Grok), Cohere, and Google (Gemma). Templates use environment variables for API configuration, making provider switching straightforward.

Do I need GPU hardware to run these AI agents?

No. Most templates use cloud-based LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) and run on standard CPU hardware. The agents make API calls to remote models, so a laptop or a $5/month VPS is sufficient for development and production deployment.

What is the difference between basic RAG and agentic RAG?

Basic RAG follows a fixed retrieve-then-generate pipeline: it searches a vector database and passes results to the LLM. Agentic RAG gives the agent control over the retrieval process — it decides when to retrieve, what queries to formulate, whether results are sufficient, and whether to re-query or correct retrieved information. Agentic RAG produces more accurate results for complex queries but requires more sophisticated orchestration.
